title: When the Tide Clock Stopped
summary: At Port Ader in 1892, a mail sloop is about to pass under a low stone arch. The tide clock promises clearance, but fourteen-year-old Tess Vale can see the sea rising. To find out which to trust, she and the clock keeper must follow the water itself.
style: Maritime linocut in midnight indigo, sea green, coral and ivory, with hand-cut hatching and letterpress dialogue strips.
coverAlt: Tess holds a coral signal flag over the harbor. Beside her, white-bearded Oren folds his arms. Behind them stands the great tide dial with its suspended float.

pages.alt: At sunrise, Tess reaches for the brass bell while small boats float alongside a stone quay. The harbor clock has a coral needle pointed low. Tess looks up at it from beside the striped wall.
pages.transcript:
Two kinds of morning
Tess: Port Ader, 1892. Every morning I hung the arch bell. The tide clock told the boats how much room they had.
Tess: Today the little punts were lifting. The needle still pointed low.

pages.alt: Tess points at the small mail sloop approaching Port Ader’s single stone arch. Oren shades his eyes. From the sloop’s wheel, its skipper raises a striped cap toward the tide tower.
pages.transcript:
The mail is early
Tess: Look at that mast, Mr Pike. Yesterday it cleared the arch by one hand.
Tess: The packet skipper tipped his cap. He had seen the clock. He hadn’t seen the stripe disappearing under the water.

pages.alt: Tess pulls the clapper rope as gulls fly past the ringing brass bell. Oren calls across the water while a deckhand loops a heavy line around the outer post, holding the mail boat short of the arch.
pages.transcript:
Three strokes
Tess: One ring meant mail. Two meant fog. I rang three, for danger. The brass jarred my teeth.
Oren: Hold at the outer post! Send your grumbles to me!

pages.alt: By lamplight, Oren opens the circular metal hatch behind the dial. A chain and brass wheel are visible on the shaft. With Oren watching, Tess turns the coral pointer away from its low position.
pages.transcript:
Inside the dial
Oren: I oiled this shaft myself before breakfast. If it’s seized, the fault is mine.
Tess: One finger moved the needle. It swung back like a spoon on a string. Nothing in the dial was stuck.

pages.alt: Tess and Oren peer over a railing at a chained cork float in the narrow well. A cutaway shows waves high against the outer wall, a submerged grille at its base, and a much lower water level in the stilling well.
pages.transcript:
The second sea
Oren: Down there is our float. The sea comes through the grille. Up goes the float and round goes the needle.
Tess: Outside, the sea had swallowed the ivory stripe. Inside, the little sea in the well was still asleep.

pages.alt: Oren empties a wooden bucket into the well as Tess watches the float. Outside, a curled dark flap covers the foot of the inlet grille. A line of bubbles escapes from underneath.
pages.transcript:
The bucket test
Tess: We poured until the well stood higher than the sea. Down by the grille, something went flap.
Tess: A little water ran out. Why couldn’t the sea run in?

pages.alt: Oren steadies a long boathook while Tess lashes a round shaving mirror to it. Beneath the quay, its reflection reveals striped cloth with a copper eyelet caught on the grille.
pages.transcript:
Under the lip
Tess: Mr Pike kept a shaving mirror above his peg. Tied to a boathook, it let us look under the lip of the quay.
Oren: That’s no seaweed. Seaweed doesn’t have a copper eyelet.

pages.alt: Tess holds the mirror close. In its reflection she recognizes three embroidered fish beside two coral stripes and a copper eyelet. She remembers a rainy market night, tying the awning to an iron ring as apples roll from a barrel.
pages.transcript:
Three fish
Tess: Three little fish in every row. I’d mended that border on our market awning all spring.
Tess: When the wind tore it, I tied the loose corner to that ring. I meant to come back for it.

pages.alt: Tess lifts a torn strip of awning by its eyelet, the stitched fish visible beside its coral bands. At the moored mail boat she faces the skipper with open hands. He offers her a coil of rope while two dockworkers listen.
pages.transcript:
Tell the pier
Tess: A torn corner had come free. I could call it storm damage, or tell the skipper the whole story.
Tess: I tied the cloth that’s blocking the clock. I’m sorry. Will you keep the boat here while we lift it?

pages.alt: Oren and Tess lean back together, hauling on the striped awning caught at the edge of the quay. Oren lays wet cloth over a blue enamel cup and presses it flat with his hand while Tess watches.
pages.transcript:
A sea with a thumb
Tess: The skipper lent us his line. Mr Pike caught the eyelet with a blunt hook. We pulled. The cloth wouldn’t budge.
Oren: The tide’s climbed again. It’s pressing the cloth flat against the grille, like my thumb on this cup.

pages.alt: Tess kneels beside a chalk drawing of two connected columns of water and holds her hands level above them. Oren lifts a wooden hatch, revealing a brass wheel on a green pipe beside a little arched channel.
pages.transcript:
An old brass wheel
Tess: If the water inside could push back just as hard, we’d only have to lift a wet rag.
Oren: The wash gate! Haven’t opened it since we scrubbed mussels off the well.

pages.alt: Oren turns the brass wash-gate wheel. A small stream runs into the well, where the tall float hangs on its chain. At the edge of the quay, Tess grips the line while the water levels match.
pages.transcript:
Level with level
Tess: I watched the wall stripes. Mr Pike opened the wash gate a finger’s width. The well filled, quietly this time.
Oren: There. Two levels, one sea. Lift now, Tess!

pages.alt: Tess lifts the sodden awning on the boathook. Oren catches the cloth below its eyelet, beside three small embroidered fish. With the dial now pointing high, five people kneel or lean to inspect the waterline itself.
pages.transcript:
Three silver tails
Tess: The awning came up inside out, heavy as a sleeping dog. Three silver tails shone through the mud.
Tess: The needle stood at high. For once, nobody clapped. We all went down to look at the water first.

pages.alt: The mail sloop passes beneath the arch, its mast clearing the stone by a small gap. Safely through, the grinning skipper shoulders a mailbag and waves to Tess and Oren on the quay.
pages.transcript:
One hand clear
Tess: We waited for the ebb. When the stripe showed again, his mast went under with one whole hand to spare.
Skipper: Tell the next port the mail’s late on account of three embroidered fish!

pages.alt: Tess kneels with a brush and paint pot to mark the quay while Oren checks the tower dial. Three little stitched fish now hang below the brass bell. Tess and Oren walk away together.
pages.transcript:
The second reading
Tess: Next morning we painted a fresh stripe on the pier. Before we rang the bell, we read the dial and the water.
Tess: I cut the three fish off the ruined cloth. They still hang from the bell rope. They’re the best knot I ever tied.
